course_description:
This course is based on the principles inherent within the Indigenous worldview that proposes Indigenous pathways to knowledge as a necessary enhancement of teaching practice and a vital component of a balanced school curriculum. This course introduces the landscape of Indigenous education in Australia as a dialogue between Indigenous and non-Indigenous ways of knowing, pedagogical practices, voices and perspectives. The course explores the terrain of Indigenous Australian studies as a curriculum area and our work as teachers in relation to Indigenous Australian students.

This course introduces you toﾠ the landscape of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander education in Australia as a dialogue between Indigenous and non-Indigenous ways of knowing, pedagogical practices, voices and perspectives. The course explores the terrain of Indigenous Australian Studies as a curriculum area and our work as teachers in relation to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students.

Each lecture aims to introduce you to important theories, philosophies and pedagogies which underpin Indigenous Australian education in both a historical and contemporary sense. The weekly tutorials make use of relational,ﾠdialogic and interactive approaches to learning which aim to engage us all in conversation and learning experiences about working effectively with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students (APST1.4), teaching Indigenous Australian Studies (APST2.4), and embedding Indigenous Australian knowledges and understandings throughout the curriculum.

Please be aware that due to cultural reasons guest lectures will not be recorded. There is often sensitive information shared by the guest lecturer about their families and it is not appropriate that it is shared through recordings. Guest lectures are also subject to change depending on guests availability.ﾠ

course_aims:
EDUC7510 aims to prepare you as initial teacher educators to work effectively and appropriately across the landscape of Indigenous Australian education. The course explores two major areas of this terrain - your work as teachers with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students, and the teaching of Indigenous Australian Studies. These aims link directly with the two Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander education focus areas of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers - Standard 1.4 which asks teachers to demonstrate strategies for teaching Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students, and Standard 2.4 which requires teachers to understand and respect Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people to promote reconciliation between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians. We aim to make space for and privilege Indigenous voices, perspectives and systems of knowledge and pedagogy as integral to our practice as teachers within the Indigenous Australian education landscape, and the set readings each week will present the work of Indigenous Australian academics and teachers in order to achieve this.

The course as a whole isﾠbuilt around threeﾠimportant concepts in relation to the Indigenous Australian education landscape: respect, relationships and reconciliation. On top of this we ask you to know yourself, know your world; know your students; and knowﾠwhat you teach. Theoretically grounded within critical pedagogy and critical race discourse with the aim of encouraging you as initial teacher educatorsﾠto consider the power and possibilities you hold to make a difference to Indigenous Australian education. We will ask you throughout the course to continually reflect upon your positioning in relation to Indigenous Australian peoples and encourage you to critique, question, and discuss the kind of teacher you would like to be in relation to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students. learning_outcomes.description: Demonstrate a critical understanding of theoretical underpinnings and debates, curriculum, legislative and policy frameworks, and pedagogical practices which make up the landscape of Indigenous education in Australia today.

Demonstrate understanding of the importance of critical and continual reflection on their professional, political and personal worldview and research-informed practices as an educator in relation to how Indigenous Australian students engage in education and learning, their peoples and cultures, and their histories and languages.
Demonstrate understanding of and reflection on Indigenous Australian education as located within broader educational frameworks, system policies, processes and contexts.
Demonstrated understandings of evidence-based teaching and learning strategies, alongside your worldview as a teacher, in relation to working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students.
Demonstrate a growing capacity to work effectively and respectfully within the Indigenous Australian education landscape.
Demonstrate the skills and knowledge to engage effectively and work in partnership with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and communities.

Work effectively and collaboratively in teams to make informed team decisions, demonstrate interpersonal, leadership and communication skills, and critically evaluate personal and peer contributions to team processes.

assessment_details.title: Reflective learning journal
assessment_details.task_description: Assessment task one requires you to complete a reflective journal outlining your learning and engagement with a range of materials and learning sources across this unit. Using the ‘Five Rs’ (Bain et al., 1999), you will undertake a process of process of critical self-reflection on your positionality to think critically about your learning, your responses to the learning and how you will take that forward into your practice as a teacher in the future. You will complete three reflections in total of 400 words each (total word count: 2000) . You must have a range of examples of learning materials including: · Lectures · Tutorial activities · Readings · Online materials and activities Reflections are to be written in short paragraphs and in first person. There must be evidence of engagement with: theories introduced throughout the unit such as critical race theory engagement of a range of course learning materials and literature including Indigenous authored sources reflection on how biases and assumptions about diverse groups and worldviews affect classroom behaviour, practices, and attitudes, and how these can adversely impact specific student groups application of the 5 Rs in reflecting on your learning experience critical reflection on your worldview (social, cultural, political, economic) and the impact upon your reaction to engaging with Indigenous Australian peoples and learning consideration of how to apply the learning from your reflection in your practice as a teacher ongoing reflexivity as a mechanism for professional development and inclusive practice Five Rs (adapted from Bain, Ballantyne, Packer & Mills, 1999) Reporting: what was the source of the learning? Responding: what were your feelings towards the issue? what was your initial response? Relating: how did the learning relate to your past and current personal and or professional experiences? why was it significant in the context of learning about Indigenous education? Reasoning: what theories are relevant in helping to understand and critically reflect on the issue? why do you think you had the initial response and what factors impacted on this? Reconstructing : why was this a significant learning experience for you as a teacher? how will you take this learning forward into practice. How does this process support your intercultural development and reflexivity? Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Indigenous Education Professional Portfolio
assessment_details.task_description: Assessment task two requires you to develop a professional portfolio, which will demonstrate your acquired knowledge in addressing the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers, in particular 1.4 and 2.4. The Australian Curriculum identifies Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and cultures as a cross-curriculum priority. The task also requires you to demonstrate your ability to embed Indigenous knowledges and perspectives in your curriculum area and discuss the theories, literature and policy that inform how and why teachers play an important role in shaping social and political discourse in Indigenous education. To do this work effectively, teachers must engage in critical self-reflection and be proactive in identifying gaps in their knowledge and skills. As part of this portfolio, you will develop a future professional learning plan that outlines your plan to engage with a range of materials and learning to continue your professional learning and development in Indigenous education. Part A (500 words) (individual task) Professional statement You will write a professional statement that outlines your commitment to improving Indigenous education outcomes and practices. This statement will demonstrate your understanding of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers, the Australian Curriculum cross-priority aimed at addressing improving Indigenous education outcomes and practices, and relevant Indigenous education policies. It will form part of your professional portfolio and should be written in first person. Your statement may include: Reference to key policy and frameworks: • The Australian Professional Standards for Teachers (including but not limited to Standards 1.4 and 2.4) • The Australian Curriculum cross-curriculum priority: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures • Relevant Indigenous education policies Your professional values: • Describe the values that guide your teaching practice (e.g., respect, inclusion, equity, cultural responsiveness) Commitment to reconciliation: • Explain how your teaching will support the process of reconciliation in education Theoretical and scholarly influences: • Reference theories, scholars, or literature that have shaped your understanding of Indigenous education (e.g., decolonising education, culturally sustaining pedagogy, Indigenist perspectives) • The importance of cultural safety, including what it can look like in a classroom context Recognition of Indigenous aspirations • Acknowledge the aspirations of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in education, such as cultural safety, academic success, and self-determination and strategies used to implement and achieve this Acknowledgement of diversity • Demonstrate an understanding of the diversity within and across First Nations peoples, including differences in culture, language, perspectives, and the historical and ongoing impacts of colonisation • Demonstrate strategies on how you will work in collaboration with local Indigenous community members to include place based Indigenous knowledges (CC 4.1.3 – practised) Part B (2000 words) (group task) Lesson plans and rationale (this task connects with Assessment task 3) In a group of three or four, develop two lesson plans that clearly demonstrate your ability to embed Indigenous Australian knowledges and perspectives into curriculum. You may use a lesson plan template used in your curriculum area, but all lesson plans must include: • Learning objectives, year level, and key learning area • Time frame • Pedagogical adjustments • Indigenous material and resources used (with evidence of rigorous selection of the type of resources used) • Practical strategies that reflect and promote cultural safety in classroom environments • Mechanisms for evaluation of the lesson Rationale The rationale is to be written in third person. It will address the reasons why it is important for teachers to be capable and confident in addressing issues in Indigenous education, including engaging effectively and collaboratively with Indigenous students, families and communities, embedding Indigenous perspectives and how to teach Indigenous students. Using scholarly sources, address the following: • Why it is important for teachers to recognise and respond to the diversity within and across First Nations peoples, including differences in culture, language, historical experience, and perspectives • Research evidence on the positive impacts of engaging with First Nations families and communities to support learning outcomes • Why it is important for teachers to engage and work in partnership with Indigenous peoples and communities to include First Nations knowledges. • How Indigenous education policy, theories, and literature can shape teaching practice • How embedding Indigenous knowledges and perspectives addresses issues in Indigenous education and broader social issues • Why cultural safety is required and strategies used to implement this in the classroom. Part C (500 words) (individual task) Indigenous Education professional development This section can be written in first person. It allows you to self-assess gaps that might still exist in your understanding of Australian histories, your culture and standpoint, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures and histories and Indigenous education frameworks and approaches. You may identify materials from a range of sources including: • Indigenous community events and organisations • Professional development sessions • Books • Web based resources • Documentaries A suggested template for your plan is available on Blackboard Ultra. assessment_details.title: Micro-teaching episode
assessment_details.due_date: 26/10/2026 - 28/10/2026 This assessment task will be conducted during scheduled tutorials.
assessment_details.other_conditions: Peer assessment factor, Secure. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: Building on your planned activity for Task 2, in your group, select key elements of your lesson plan and teach a condensed version of the lesson. This task gives you an opportunity to trial and refine your lesson plan by translating your ideas into practice within a microteaching context. It provides a chance to receive feedback on your planned strategies for embedding Indigenous Australian knowledges and perspectives. The task also includes a structured peer interaction component, where you respond to questions and engage in professional discussion to justify and strengthen your teaching decisions. Part A: Microteaching episode (approx. 10 minutes) In your group, your teaching must demonstrate: · Clear learning objectives appropriate to the chosen year level and learning area · Meaningful and accurate inclusion of Indigenous Australian knowledges and perspectives · Use of carefully selected Indigenous resources/materials · Culturally safe teaching practices, including respectful language and representation · Appropriate pedagogical strategies (e.g., scaffolding, questioning, modelling) · Pedagogical adjustments to support diverse learners · Active student engagement strategies Part B: Professional Explanation and Interaction (approx. 5 minutes) Following your microteaching, your group will participate in a short whole-class interaction (Q&A and discussion). Your group will be expected to: · Briefly explain the intent and context of the lesson · Justify your selection of Indigenous perspectives and resources · Explain how your teaching promotes cultural safety and respect · Describe how the lesson could be adapted for different learners · Respond thoughtfully and professionally to peer and tutor questions How this is marked: This task is a Pass/Fail hurdle for the course. Your group will receive a single mark for this task and you will be provided with a copy of the Pass/Fail rubric in advance. This assessment will be recorded in line with academic policy. learning_activities.topic: Introducing Indigenous knowledges and education In this tutorial, pre-service teachers will explore course requirements, begin building relational connections, and use the 5 Rs to critically reflect on how their social, cultural and historical experiences shape their worldviews and classroom practice (CC 4.2.2 – practised).

Introducing Indigenous knowledges and education This lecture introduces pre-service teachers to the landscape of Indigenous education, including the importance of Indigenous knowledges, positionality, appropriate language, and the key theories and policies that inform teaching practice (CC 4.1.2 and CC 4.2.1 – taught).

Worldviews In this tutorial, pre-service teachers will critically reflect on their connections, identities and worldviews, exploring how social, cultural and historical experiences shape their understanding of students and their developing teaching practice (CC 4.2.1 and CC 4.2.2 – practised).

Worldviews This lecture supports preservice teachers to examine their identities, worldviews, privilege and connections, and to consider how these shape their teaching practices and relationships with diverse students (CC 4.2.1 and CC 4.2.2 – taught).

Australian histories - how much do we really know? In this tutorial, preservice teachers critically examine Australian histories, reflect on how their knowledge has been shaped, and explore the ongoing impacts of colonisation and hidden histories in schooling (CC 4.1.2 – practised).

QLD Histories and the importance of communities: In this guest lecture, Aunty Denise Proud shares lived experience of past Queensland policies and life at Cherbourg, supporting pre-service teachers to understand local histories, their ongoing impacts, and the importance of engaging respectfully with First Nations communities and families (CC 4.1.1, CC 4.1.3 and CC 4.1.5 – taught).

Equity and Equality in the classroom In this tutorial, pre-service teachers examine race and racism in Australian schools, analyse classroom scenarios, and develop strategies for embedding First Nations perspectives and fostering culturally inclusive teaching practice (CC 4.2.3 – practised).

Equity & Equality This lecture examines racism within Australian education systems and supports pre-service teachers to identify personal and systemic biases, evaluate curriculum decisions, and develop strategies that foster culturally inclusive classrooms and support Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students (CC 4.2 – taught).

Hidden Histories Crossing Cultures In this tutorial, pre-service teachers begin developing lesson plans that embed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander perspectives on Australian history within a selected key learning area (CC 4.1.1 – practised).

Hidden Histories Crossing Cultures This lecture explores Australian history through Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander perspectives, using artwork and storytelling to deepen pre-service teachers’ understanding of hidden histories, colonisation, and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Histories and Cultures cross-curriculum priority (CC 4.1 – taught).

Curriculum is not neutral In this tutorial, preservice teachers critically examine how curriculum values, assumptions and biases shape the learning experiences and sense of belonging of Indigenous Australian students and consider implications for inclusive professional practice (CC 4.2.4 – practised).

Curriculum is not neutral This lecture examines how values, knowledges, beliefs and biases shape curriculum design, and supports pre-service teachers to make informed decisions about embedding Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander perspectives in inclusive and culturally responsive ways (CC 4.1 and CC 4.2 – taught).

Black is... In this tutorial, pre-service teachers examine how policies such as the Certificate of Exemption shaped Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander identities and consider how teachers can affirm and support the identities of young people in schools (CC 4.1.5 – practised).

The Stolen Generations & exemption certificate This lecture examines the Stolen Generations and the Certificate of Exemption, exploring how past policies shaped the lives, identities and experiences of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and continue to influence education today (CC 4.1 – taught).

Policy and professional practice In this tutorial, pre-service teachers connect key Indigenous education policy objectives with their developing professional values, commitments and teaching practice through work on their professional statement.

Indigenous education policy This lecture examines international, national and state Indigenous education policies and considers how key priorities—including connection to culture, high expectations and meaningful pathways—inform culturally responsive practice in schools.

Selecting curriculum materials: In this hands-on tutorial, pre-service teachers use the YARNS framework to critically evaluate curriculum materials and select appropriate resources for embedding Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledges and perspectives (CC 4.1.1 – practised).

Critical selection of curriculum resources: This lecture examines how media narratives influence understandings of Indigenous education and supports preservice teachers to identify and critically evaluate quality curriculum materials for embedding Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledges and perspectives.

Building Partnerships & co-constructing curriculum In this tutorial, preservice teachers explore the phases of co-constructing learning experiences and consider how collaboration with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities can support culturally authentic and relevant curriculum design (CC 4.1 – practised).

Building Partnerships & co-constructing curriculum This lecture explores research-informed frameworks for embedding Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander perspectives, with a focus on collaboration and co-design with First Nations communities to support culturally authentic and relevant classroom practice (CC 4.1 – taught).

Practicing culturally responsive teaching In this tutorial, preservice teachers practise culturally responsive teaching strategies and reflect on how cultural safety, awareness and respectful pedagogies can be enacted in classroom practice (CC 4.1.4 – practised).

Culturally Responsive Teaching This lecture explores culturally responsive pedagogies that draw on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students’ cultures, identities, experiences and perspectives, with a focus on creating culturally safe and respectful classroom practice (CC 4.1 – taught).
